To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the WTI tumor‐suppressor candidate gene does not appear to play a role in ovarian tumorigenesi, and that WTI gene expression may play a role in the control of the cell cycle.

(a) the WTI gene is not altered at the DNA level, (b) WTI mRNA levels are variable and do not correlate with allelic losses on chromosome 11, and (c) WTI/p53 interaction may play a role in ovarian tumorigenesi.

(1) the WTI gene does not appear to function as a classical tumor suppressor gene in the ovarian tumors studied, and (2) the observed allelic deletions on 11 p 12–13 may be the consequence of a “second hit,” possibly a recessive oncogene.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the WTI tumor‐suppressor candidate gene in ovarian tumors.
the identification and characterization of genes that are involved in human ovarian tumorigeness.

the identification of the molecular mechanisms possibly affecting WT 1 function in human epithelial ovarian tumors and the possible functional consequences of such mechanisms on ovarian tumor progression and prognosis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
WTI gene alterations are not involved in the genesis or development of ovarian tumors, and that the WTI expression levels in ovarian tumors are not directly related to their biological behavior.
, at present, the WTI gene cannot be considered a classical tumor‐suppressing gene in ovarian cancer and, therefore, its involvement in the pathogenesis of these tumors is not yet established.
WTI is not a classical tumor‐suppresser gene, but rather a gene that plays a crucial role in the development of the human female reproductive system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the WTI tumor‐suppressor hypothesis is not supported by our data.
WTI expression is not altered in human ovarian tumors and that the allelic loss on chromosome 11p 13 does not seem to be associated with a WTI gene defect.
the WTI tumor suppressor gene is not involved in the pathogenesis of ovarian cancers, but the WT1 gene may be a potential target for therapeutic interventions in ovarian cancers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the WTI oncogene is not a classical tumor suppressor gene in human ovarian tumors, as previously hypothesized.
the Wilms tumor gene is not involved in the development of ovarian tumors.
WTI is expressed in ovarian tumors, and that its expression may be modulated at the transcriptional level, possibly by the p53 protein.
